newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions threaten new strike on labor laws.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions threaten new strike on labor laws.

text.p: Argentine unions threatened Peronist President Carlos Menem on Thursday with another general strike, this time for up to 48 hours, if he goes ahead with plans for new labour laws and union healthcare deregulation.
Unions staged a 24-hour strike in August and a 36-hour walkout last week, which they said was a 95 percent success but Menem mocked as "tourism" or an excuse for a long weekend.

But the protest against 17.1 percent unemployment, fiscal austerity moves and benefit cuts was given fresh impetus by Menem's rush to modernise labour laws and deregulate union health funds, which earn them $2.5 billion a year.

The head of the main CGT labour federation, Rodolfo Daer, said before a strategy meeting: "We don't rule out a strike or any other measures necessary to reject any initiatives on labour flexibility and the deregulation of health funds."
Hugo Moyano, head of the hardline MTA union faction, said he was going to propose a 48 hour stoppage.

And CGT director Armando Cavalieri threatened to get tough if Menem carried out his threat to push the laws through by decree. "The right road is parliament. If they do it by decree that is confrontation for confrontation's sake," he said.

But the government, which argued that modernising labour laws was the only way to fight unemployment, steamed ahead with its reform plans. Jorge Matzkin, Peronist whip in the lower house of Congress, said in a debate on jobs late Wednesday that people should not expect miracle cures.
"The solutions are not going to come out of here like a string of sausages," said the lawmaker.

Labour Minister Armando Caro Figueroa said after Thursday's weekly cabinet meeting, "The government is convinced that if we don't change now, jobs won't grow at the rate we need to beat unemployment. To solve Argentina's unemployment problem we have to create 500,000 jobs a year."
The economy needs to grow at 5-6 percent a year to create jobs -- "something we are managing despite the strikes, which are an incredible attack on economic growth," he said.
Menem wants to dismantle union control on collective wage negotations, swap redundancy pay for unemployment insurance and make wages variable depending on the economic climate.
